title: Strain-tunable van Hove singularity and superconducting dome in monolayer kagome metal CsTi$_3$Bi$_5$
authors: Run Lv, Wenqian Tu, Dingfu Shao, Yuping Sun, Wenjian Lu
abstract: The recently discovered titanium-based kagome metal CsTi$_3$Bi$_5$, which exhibits superconductivity without an accompanying charge density wave, provides an ideal platform to investigate the intrinsic electronic structure and superconductivity. Moreover, it enables the exploration of superconductivity in the two-dimensional limit of the kagome lattice. Here, we systematically investigate the influence of biaxial mechanical strain ($\varepsilon$) on the electronic structure and superconductivity of monolayer CsTi$_3$Bi$_5$ using first-principles calculations. We demonstrate that the prominent van Hove singularity (VHS) at the M point can be monotonically tuned to the Fermi level by tensile strain. Furthermore, the superconducting transition temperature $T_C$ exhibits a dome-shaped dependence on strain, reaching a maximum of 3.6 K at an optimal tensile strain of $\varepsilon=+2\%$. The average superconducting gap magnitude is 0.35 meV, with an orbital-dependent and anisotropic distribution. Our results provide a detailed understanding of the superconductivity of monolayer CsTi$_3$Bi$_5$ and show that strain is an effective, continuous tuning knob for manipulating the electronic structure and superconductivity.
summary: This theoretical study uses first-principles calculations to explore how mechanical strain affects the superconductivity of the kagome metal CsTi3Bi5. Researchers found that applying tensile strain can tune the electronic structure by shifting a Van Hove singularity to the Fermi level. This tuning leads to a maximum superconducting transition temperature of 3.6 K at an optimal strain of +2%, demonstrating strain's potential as a powerful control parameter.
main_problem: The study investigates how biaxial mechanical strain influences the electronic structure and superconductivity of the kagome metal CsTi3Bi5.
main_result: Tensile strain tunes the Van Hove singularity (VHS) to the Fermi level and induces a dome-shaped superconducting transition temperature (Tc), peaking at 3.6 K at +2% strain.
method: The research employs first-principles calculations (DFT) combined with electron-phonon coupling (EPC) theory to model the superconducting properties.
model_or_system: The system is the monolayer kagome metal CsTi3Bi5, which is studied in the two-dimensional limit. The calculations systematically vary the in-plane lattice parameters to apply controlled biaxial strain.
key_observables: Van Hove Singularity (VHS) shift, superconducting transition temperature (Tc), average superconducting gap magnitude (Delta), and electron-phonon coupling strength (lambda).
important_parameters: Biaxial strain (epsilon), optimal tensile strain (+2%), and the resulting maximum Tc of 3.6 K.
main_assumptions: The study assumes the out-of-plane coordinates of certain atoms are relaxed, and it uses the Allen-Dynes modified McMillan equation for Tc estimation.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the evolution of the band structure and VHS with strain, the phonon spectra and mode-resolved EPC strength vs. strain, and the resulting dome-shaped Tc dependence on strain.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of first establishing the material as a promising platform, then systematically applying strain via DFT calculations to track the electronic structure changes (VHS tuning), followed by calculating the resulting superconducting properties (Tc and gap) using EPC theory.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter superconductivity, the concept of using external strain as a continuous, tunable knob to manipulate electronic band structure and enhance emergent quantum phenomena (superconductivity) is a general principle relevant to controlling quantum states in engineered systems.
